Longer-articles/If-anyone-builds-it,-eve.title: If anyone builds it, everyone dies... or not
Longer-articles/If-anyone-builds-it,-eve.content:
A couple of days ago I finished “If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies”, by Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares. I bought the book when visiting New York City last year and I had the chance to get my hands on a signed edition by Nate Soares. I didn’t start reading it right away, though, and it sat forgotten on my shelves until last week, when I had an interesting discussion with some friends and was a bit surprised to see that they were genuinely worried about AI doom.
A few years ago I spent a few months very seriously thinking about this and I ended up concluding that the reasons to worry were probably an exaggeration. But a few years ago we didn’t have ChatGPT, image or video generation was not even a thing, and practically nobody had heard about Anthropic or Dario Amodei. Today the landscape has changed radically: ChatGPT is solving open problems in mathematics, image and video generation are solved problems, and we have Claude finding vulnerabilities in systems that were thought to be completely safe. With these rapid developments I think it is fair to revisit whether my point of view has changed or not.
I am not going to repeat here the arguments for AI doom because they are widely discussed everywhere and I don’t think I will do it better than others. What I think makes sense is to start by clarifying where I stand. I think that:

AI will eventually be better at ALL mental tasks than any human. In fact, I believe we are 95% there. The remaining 5% gap will be closed in the next 2 to 3 years. I do not think it is possible to believe otherwise unless you come from a non-materialistic perspective, which would make the discussion about something totally different. To me, humans are slightly more intelligent than chimpanzees but still made of flesh and limited by their biology. It should be no surprise whatsoever that a machine can replicate and improve human thought, including its creativity and imagination.
AI will be powerful. An ASI will be capable of quickly conceiving new technologies (some of them we can’t even fathom today), and also making fundamental advances in fields like mathematics, biology or physics. I expect proofs for P != NP, new fundamental theories of physics and mechanistic models of how complex development programs are encoded in DNA.
AI will not be aligned with our goals by default. Some ASIs might be agentic and have goals that are alien to us. Some ASIs might plot and conspire to reach those goals. And they might be very good at that.

With the beliefs above, it seems quite obvious that I should just jump to the same conclusions as the authors. So, where do I disagree and what are the problems I have with the authors’ stance?
The main issue I have is that they speak with a level of certainty that is unwarranted. They consistently present theoretical scenarios as inevitable. The full argumentation relies on many steps going the way they predict, and the reasons why it could go a different way are simply not presented or even dismissed. The reasons they give for the individual steps are in fact quite weaker than they seem.
To be clear, the book gets important things right. I think that a sufficiently capable agent with goals alien to ours would be dangerous, and the field probably deserves more attention than it currently gets. My quarrel is not with any of that. It is with the leap from “this could go very wrong” to “this will kill everyone.”
I see three problems with the argument: their model of power, their model of the world, and the way the argument is built.
Power is more than intelligence
Complex power dynamics
The main scenario that the authors worry about is a rogue AI taking over from some data center and successfully killing humanity. But they do not discuss at all the most likely scenario, which is the one in which, if machines are agentic and intelligent enough to achieve such a feat, there will be multiple machines involved. This possibility (which is the most likely one, given the number of companies developing different AIs and how close they are) is simply not considered.
Today, the most powerful entities on the planet are complex agents that go by the name of States. States control populations by using narratives that make them legitimate in the eyes of a big fraction of their subjects. States are growing in power and reach all over the world. Yudkowsky and Soares focus all of their attention on intelligence and its consequences, and pay zero attention to the real dynamics of the incredibly powerful agents that exist today.
For every example the authors can come up with about how intelligence wins, we can come up with many others in which intelligence does not win unless it is accompanied by many other factors that are essential. Heisenberg was a top physicist but the Nazis did not manage to make the bomb. The USA had absolute superiority over Vietnam and still lost the war. We can envision an ASI developing futuristic technology for specific states, and that technology being deployed to either conquer Taiwan or do something similar. But we can also envision a race of different ASIs that develop independent goals and seek political power to obtain them.
The scenario the authors describe requires many things to play out in a specific way. Namely, it requires that machines converge on activities that are hostile to humans, and that machines (or a sufficient number of them) successfully coordinate among themselves. The standard response is that machines converge on killing humans because you are made of atoms, and machines don’t want to kill you, but they want your atoms. Which is a slogan for an argument that can be developed with more words, but it is still a slogan and not that deep. In a world where multiple machines are fighting for power, aren’t machines made of atoms too? If we can predict with certainty that machines will be hostile to humans, why do we assume that machines will successfully coordinate among themselves? And note that multipolar systems are precisely the ones in which weak actors tend to survive. Tiny states persist between great powers, and entire species persist alongside us, not because anyone protects them, but because eliminating them costs more than it is worth to any single player busy competing with the others. A world of machines fighting each other for atoms is not obviously a world with no room left for us.
Intelligence is not everything
In the words of the authors:

“Human intelligence is the source of all our power, all our technology. Even within the human species, small differences in how long groups spend accumulating technological prowess translates into military advantages on the order of ‘We have guns and they do not.’ Between species, the disparity in power conferred by intelligence is more acute: Individual chimpanzees sometimes kill individual humans, but there is a reason why our species is trying to protect their species from being accidentally extinguished.”

For the authors, intelligence is power. But we should remember that Einstein did not conquer the world. Neither did Von Neumann. Very intelligent people are routinely outmaneuvered and outsmarted by individuals and coalitions with more political ability. Power is a multifactorial phenomenon in which intelligence is one of the variables, but not the only one. Take Afghanistan. The United States had overwhelming military and technological superiority over the Taliban and occupied the country for twenty years. The moment it left, the Taliban were back in power. Raw superiority did not translate into lasting control.
I find it telling that the analogies presented in the book as examples of what humans could be up against when fighting an ASI are in fact good counterexamples. Take the one of the Aztecs:

“Our best guess is that a superintelligence will come at us with weird technology that we didn’t even think was possible, that we didn’t understand was allowed by the rules. That is what has usually happened when groups with different levels of technological capabilities meet. It’d be like the Aztecs facing down guns. It’d be like a cavalry regiment from 1825 facing down the firepower of a modern military.”

The Spaniards did not defeat the Aztecs because they had guns or cannons (though that certainly helped). The Spaniards defeated the Aztecs because they were politically cunning enough to lead a coalition of indigenous forces against a common enemy. The Spaniards, in spite of having much better technology than the indigenous Americans, “failed” at conquering technologically less developed societies such as the Maya or the Mapuche. Of course, one could argue that this is just an illustrative example, and perhaps a more suitable one would be a group of monkeys fighting a group of Navy SEALs. But this would quickly become a tennis match of reference classes. The thing I want to stress is that one of the examples they keep using multiple times is in fact a pretty good counterexample of why technology by itself does not necessarily lead to a guaranteed victory.
A more interesting and richer analogy could have been studying the dynamics that played out after the Opium Wars. In that case, a very minor state from far away was able to defeat a much more powerful enemy. And what happened then? Did England ever manage to get absolute and total domination of the world? Not really, or at least not for long. As soon as other powerful agents saw the result of using cannons, they did not stay put: they moved accordingly and adapted. Japan went from a feudal society to a major superpower in record time. And soon, the power gap that England had created thanks to its technology was closed.
The world is not a small world
In the book Radical Uncertainty, John Kay and Mervyn King criticize the use of mathematical models and simplified scenarios (what they call “Small Worlds”) to make predictions about reality. In a small world there are clearly defined rules and there is predictability. For example, Chess is a small world game; Go is a small world game. A sufficiently good machine will always outplay a human because the game is deterministic and has clearly defined settings. Backgammon, on the other hand, has a probabilistic component. Playing optimally does not necessarily lead to a victory (the advantage only shows up when the game is repeated many times).
In the real world, seizing power and wielding it is a game that looks much less like chess than we normally think. There are physical limitations to what can be predicted or not, and even completely deterministic systems are subject to behaviors that are impossible to foresee in the long run. This does not make planning or executing “impossible”, it just makes it way less certain. So when the authors keep using the chess metaphor and how machines will just win because they are better at everything, I think they are heavily discounting the inherent unpredictability that we have in the real world for no good reason. This, to me, is the central objection, and it does not depend on any claim that the two sides are evenly matched. Even an agent vastly more capable than us cannot compute its way through a system that is irreducibly unpredictable. A bigger brain does not turn a small world into a large one. The limits on prediction are in the world, not in the size of the mind facing it.
Time is swept under the rug
To the point above it could be argued that we might not know the intermediate steps but machines will win in the long run, because they do not need to be perfect at everything, they just need to be better. I think that is a weak argument. The authors are concerned with something that happens in the next few years (it could be 10, 20 or 30).
I have no idea what the world will look like in 500 years. Probably nothing like what we expect. Maybe once we find out how to transfer minds to machines, humanity eventually dissolves into a digital realm where it is free from diseases and aging, and we even decide to abandon our individuality to merge into some sort of single giant creature. Or maybe nothing like that happens. But I do agree that “humanity” can drastically change in the long run.
An unfalsifiable, ill-defined argument
Intelligence as a binary thing
The authors present ASI as a binary thing, something that you get once you reach a threshold. Clearly, Yudkowsky and Soares are both very intelligent and respectable people and know that intelligence exists on a spectrum. But they nonetheless treat ASI as something that you get once you cross a magic threshold of no return. This binary sort of thinking is exemplified most clearly in the example of the nuclear bomb:

“The critical number governing a nuclear reactor is the neutron multiplication factor… The critical threshold is 100 percent: Anything below that peters out, and anything above that cascades. Then at 100.65 percent, the cascade no longer depends on delayed neutrons, and goes out of control.”

This steers the conversation into the wrong framing. The analogy smuggles in the assumption that intelligence is a one-dimensional quantity with a critical point, and that is precisely the thing in dispute. Machines can be incredibly clever at some things and still silly or non-agentic at others.
A failure of imagination
Many of the arguments are presented as certain when in fact they involve multiple inferential steps where alternative scenarios are possible, but these other scenarios are not discussed. For example, the authors state that the alignment problem must be solved in one shot, because there will be only one opportunity to solve it. But they do not seem to contemplate the possibility that before reaching an ASI that successfully kills everyone, there might be machines that first try to grab power and harm humans and fail. Or maybe they do contemplate it, but then they dismiss it as not truly an ASI.
I know that the common reply to this observation is:
“Oh, but it does not need to be perfect or all-mighty, it just needs to be good enough!”
But I think this leads us to an impasse. I do not know what “good enough” means, and I can see many scenarios that don’t end up with everything dying, and which are not necessarily mutually exclusive. For example:

Machines keep getting better and better but multiple entities are developed, resulting in a sort of dynamic equilibrium of power (just as we have multiple states today).
Machines keep getting better and better, and with their help we successfully learn how to create institutions that protect human life better than our current institutions do.
Some machines go rogue and start trying to cause havoc, but other machines fight against those machines.
Different societal bottlenecks make the development of truly powerful machines much slower than predicted: bureaucratic regulations, disruption of logistic lines, terrorist attacks against specific datacenters, and so on.
Machines develop the technology to scan human brains in a way that can be uploaded to some cloud and preserved there.

The usual move when you raise any of these is to define them away. It is a No True Scotsman in disguise:

What happens if the machine first tries to control a bio-lab but fails and makes all alarms go off? Oh, in that case it won’t be an ASI.
What happens if the machine fails at escaping the security measures that other, more intelligent machines have prepared? Oh, in that case it won’t be an ASI.
What happens if machines are never capable of planning much further ahead than us in the high-complexity environment that the world is? Oh, in that case it won’t be an ASI.

This makes the whole argument about ASI impossible to reason about and unfalsifiable. When confronted with the fact that some things might not be possible, the authors always seem to get away with:
“Oh, but an ASI would find a way to do this, the way [insert clever example] did.”
To which I would say: well, you have a belief in which a genie in the lamp is among us and is able to do anything, but there might be some things that are not even possible for the genie. This is a very dangerous argument because it is already armored against any criticism.
If I ask a doomer to generate a plausible scenario, it goes like this:
A machine does X, Y, W and then finds that doing Z will kill all humanity.
I point out: X is unrealistic because of A, B, C.
I get the reply: oh, but this is just an example, an ASI would “know” how to do that.
This is impossible to falsify. The result is that you are using your imagination’s limitations as an argument that “something” is possible, which I find an example of terrible epistemics. The fact that we fail to imagine should point towards decreasing the likelihood of doom scenarios, not the other way around.
What does it even mean to solve alignment?
Every time I read about alignment as a problem that can be “solved”, like the Riemann hypothesis, I feel that the field is terribly confused. Let’s imagine for a second that we treated the problem of making a house safe the way we treat the alignment problem nowadays:
Q: I think this house is sufficiently safe, we put a gate with a powerful lock. A: Oh, it’s not safe because someone could break a window. Q: Well, the house is on the 7th floor and the windows are not easy to reach. A: Oh, but what would happen if someone went to the rooftop and then bungee-jumped from there? Q: Well, that’s unlikely because it would require first opening the rooftop door, and that is also safe. A: Oh, but what would happen if someone rented the adjacent house and tried to carve a hole through the wall? Q: Well, that’s unlikely because (1) you would need to be able to rent that place, and (2) you would make a ton of noise that would probably alert all the neighbors, even if the operation happened while the owner of the house was not there. A: Oh, but what would happen if someone rented all the adjacent houses and drugged all the neighbors so that he could dig safely without being heard?
…
(this can continue ad infinitum)
This can always continue because nothing can be claimed to be 100% safe, just as I suspect you can’t claim agents to be 100% aligned. (I do not think even different modules of our own brain are “aligned”, whatever that means.) Or take the example of making a cryptocurrency safe. Is Bitcoin safe? A demigod will always find ways to break things, no matter how safe you make something.
The only reason someone would think about alignment on a binary scale is because they are deeply thinking of ASI as a binary thing. To me, alignment is something ill-defined that probably exists in many dimensions. Agents pursue goals, but those goals might change over time. Agents form coalitions and alliances. Why are those things not discussed? Alignment is presented as something that can be solved, when in fact the most likely thing is that it will follow rules very similar to the power-grasping rules that already exist in politics.

Conclusion
In the 18th century Blaise Pascal reasoned that it was better to believe in God than to be an atheist, because in the case that God does exist (no matter how unlikely that is), you would be better off by believing in it. I think this is an evil argument that can be used to justify any behavior. Given that there is a risk of X happening, and X is really bad, then Y (no matter what Y is) is justified. The authors are making a sophisticated version of this argument. And I do not question their integrity or their reasons: I do think they are honest and they are just acting in the best possible ways given their beliefs.
I would have no problem if the book were titled Some Potential Risks of Developing AI, or something similar. But the book is not called that. The book is called “If anyone builds it, everyone dies”. You could think that this is just a marketing strategy, but it is not, it does reflect what the authors think and discuss inside. In general, I do think that AI safety is an important field and probably requires more attention than we currently give it. But there is a far cry between saying this and what these authors are saying: let’s bomb datacenters that are being used to train AIs.
To me truth should always be a point of reference. If the probability of human extinction is 1%, let’s discuss it as it is: a small probability of a catastrophe. If the probability is higher and the potential damage is smaller, let’s also treat it for what it is.
Having accurate beliefs about the world should be something we all strive for. If we stop doing this, we would just live in small concrete cubicles, avoid human contact and obsess over the tiniest speck of dust.
The authors do end on a positive note. “Where there is life, there is hope”. But this feels more like a last-minute addendum made by the editor to avoid making the book really depressing. You can’t call a book “everyone dies” and expect a positive message. The only thing I can say is that, whenever there is a controversial issue, I like hearing the best arguments on both sides and trying to make up my own mind. From Yudkowsky I did learn that it is at least one order of magnitude easier to identify who is right in an academic discussion than to reach those conclusions yourself. I approached the book with some fear and I leave it now thinking that the arguments for AI doom are weaker than I expected.

Longer-articles/Presenting-ZOMBI2.title: Presenting ZOMBI2
Longer-articles/Presenting-ZOMBI2.content:
The story of Zombi (let’s call it ZOMBI1 for clarity) is as it follows: just after finished my PhD, after working for many months on my thesis manuscript, I kind of missed writing code. It sounds strange and it probably is, but that’s what I did almost right away after presenting my dissertation on lateral gene transfers to date the tree of life.
So I worked for about a year or so in ZOMBI1. I think I rewrote it about 3 times, each time slightly better than the previous iteration, incorporating more functions and options. The end result was not fantastic and I think that the code is less than pretty, but we ended up publishing it in the journal Bioinformatics and some people has used it over the years. To me it always was an exercise for my own understanding. Richard P. Feynman said (and I fully agree), that if you are not able to build something, you do not understand it; ZOMBI1 was for me a way to show to myself that I had truly understood the phylogenetic reconciliations we were using to understand genome evolution.
The last month I have been working almost non-stop on doing a full rewrite of ZOMBI in what is called now ZOMBI2, assisted with Claude Opus 4.8. I spent about a week of intensive work to have something much bigger, better documented and complete in general than the previous version. I spent about three weeks trimming it down, cutting down fat and removing many bad decisions that the LLMs do automatically. Do not get me wrong: if it weren’t for Claude I would have simply not started doing this project because it would have taken me about 10-20x longer, and the result would not have been half as good.
The experience of developing ZOMBI2 has been totally different from the first one. In the first version I was tackling problems one by one, writing the code myself. In this one, I have been giving very specific feedback mostly in English (both very high level and very low level), revising every decision very closely and spending a lot of time simplifying things. Claude has a massive tendency to overcomplicate things unnecessarily, with jargon and sentences that are simply not human-readable. If you do not keep it on a very short leash, you end up with something that might work but it is terrible spagueti code very difficult to maintain and to expand in an organized and organic way.
I am in general, very satisfied with the result, although is not over yet. I still need to add some more features, tests and documentation plus, writing the paper. However, the hardest part is now behind. This is a platform that I will maintain over the years and that I know I can safely use to produce new results in an environment that I am highly familiar with.

Longer-articles/Science-is-less-determin.title: Science is less deterministic than you think
Longer-articles/Science-is-less-determin.content:
This is a comment on the paper Same data, different analysts
Unless you have been living under a rock, you know that we are in the midst of what historians may one day call “The Replication Crisis Era”.
Long story short, starting in the 2000s, some scientists started ringing the alarms that many (if not a majority) of published scientific papers could be inaccurate, misleading, or simply wrong. People started reporting examples of a practice called “p-hacking”, in which the data is “adjusted” until significant p-values start popping out. I am not talking about specific instances of a lone scientist that had committed fraud or simply lied about his results but of a systemic problem that seemed to pervade modern science. In 2015, a landmark paper published in Science (Estimating the reproducibility of Psychological Science) revealed that, after reanalyzing a set of 100 psychology papers from 3 high impact factor journals, fewer than 50% of the papers could be reproduced. Around this time, multiple groups studied this phenomenon and most of the blame was put on the fact that many studies had low sample sizes, making them prone to noise.
But years passed and while it is clear that part of the problem has to do with small sample sizes, thinking that the issue is only about data collection depicts a very incomplete picture. The variability is not related to the data alone, but also to how we handle the data. Gould et al. have published an excellent paper illustrating this. The setting is:
There are two datasets and one scientific question for each of them:



The first is the “blue tit” dataset , which comes from a three-year study of wild birds nesting at Wytham Wood in the UK. It includes information about 3,720 chicks across 452 broods, with information like the weight and tarsus length of nestlings 14 days after hatching, the number of siblings they had, and the size of their parents. The question analysts had to answer was: To what extent is nestling growth influenced by competition with siblings?




The second is the “Eucalyptus” dataset, derived from the Bush Returns program in Victoria, Australia. It consists of 351 quadrants surveyed across 18 different sites. Researchers were interested in reforestation on private land, and the specific question for analysts was: How does grass cover influence Eucalyptus spp. seedling recruitment?



It is important to note that both datasets involved experimental interventions, not just passive observation. In the bird study, researchers performed “cross-fostering” (moving chicks between nests to artificially enlarge or reduce brood sizes). This allowed them to isolate the effect of sibling competition from genetic factors. In the Eucalyptus study, the intervention was the removal of livestock grazing to see if the canopy would regenerate naturally. I highlight this because some people could argue that the problem is not so much about reproducibility but about observational vs interventional studies in general.
Now, the impressive part is this: The researchers recruited a massive group of 246 analysts across 173 teams to investigate these questions. Not only this, they also found a very large group of reviewers that evaluated the reliability of the statistical methods (without seeing the results) of each analysis. To make the results comparable, each analyst team was required to report a standardized effect size that would summarize how strong the effect was (and the direction).
The results?
Judge for yourself:

Figure 2 from the paper, which captures the main results
To simplify, what we are seeing is:

Every horizontal line represents a different analysis from a different analyst group.
The x-axis is the “strength” of the correlation between (A) growth and competition from siblings, (B) number of seedlings and percentage of grass.

In other words, values to the left suggest a negative relation, while values to the right suggest a positive relation. For A, most studies find a negative relation, though the magnitude changes substantially for many of them. For B, the results are more balanced; some find a very negative relation while others find a clear positive signal.
So, how does this bode for the replicability of science? Remember, we are dealing with an almost perfect scenario where everyone has access to the same dataset! Some friends of mine saw this and thought the glass was half full: at least in the birds dataset, most teams seem to recover a negative relation, though for the Eucalyptus it is less clear. For me, the glass is half empty. It is true that in the birds there was a clear majority in one direction, but the magnitude of the effect seems to vary almost continuously across a wide range of values. And in the Eucalyptus case, the values seem to be all over the place!
There also seemed to be very little consensus among reviewers about what constituted a good scientific approach! Some reviewers would classify one paper as “Publishable as it is” while others would call it “Unpublishable”. When removing those papers that had received marks of “Unpublishable” and “Major Revisions”, the remaining analyses still seemed not to agree on their conclusions. Similar results also happened when the analyses coming from people who had no self-identified expertise in statistics were removed.
So the obvious question once might ask is, where does the variability come from? Well, it seems to stem from the fact that seemingly clear scientific questions are instead pretty vague and can be translated into numbers in many different ways. Maybe an example clarifies this: let’s say that we want to measure growth (in the example of the birds). What do we use as a proxy? The weight? Or the size of the legs? Or should we combine both into a single variable? Should both have the same importance? Or should the importance be weighted? Another factor to consider is: what do we do with outliers? Traditional teaching says that in some cases they should be removed. But another solution is using statistical methods (such as non-parametric testing) that are more robust to outliers. Or should we include them (or some of them?) because they are in fact the observations containing the most information? Any of these solutions is perfectly defensible in isolation, but a proper statistical analysis can contain many of these questions that can be answered in different ways, leading in the end to quite different results.
Now, what should we conclude from this? I am not sure there is a single lesson from this paper, but it does provide some bits to update our posterior towards a region of more skepticism in general with scientific papers. I already try to be very selective with what I read because most papers are just a waste of time. To me It goes without saying, but I do not think we need to throw our hands up in despair and become postmodernists. Science has a very good track record of discovering truths and producing an accurate map of the world that surrounds us. But, believing blindly in the powers of peer-review and statistical analyses as many science fanboys do, it is equally mistaken. I was aware of this, this is an extra point in that direction.
The questions that scientists analyzed in this study were totally aseptic (or as close as they can be). Most people will not care about whether grass is more or less important for the growth of Eucalyptus. Now, if this is the level of disagreement we find in a neutral topic with a perfect dataset, should we be surprised when, in controversial topics such as the impact of the minimum wage on the labor market, people obtain contradictory results? I was swayed by reading Bernoulli’s fallacy to believe that a large part of the problem is our very flawed box of statistical tools. Although I still believe that a more widespread use of Bayesian analysis would remove some of the constant pernicious problems that keep bugging us, now I see that the problem is also in the intrinsic “vagueness” of the world around us and this is not leaving us at any point soon.

Longer-articles/Simulating-an-alien-faun.title: Simulating an Alien Fauna
Longer-articles/Simulating-an-alien-faun.content:
For the past few days, I have been simulating a population of “aliens” to create original teaching materials for an upcoming phylogenetics workshop. While I initially considered using the classic Caminalcules (a group of imaginary creatures created by the evolutionary biologist Joseph H. Camin in the 1960s) I decided to develop a dataset from scratch. To me, using an artificial dataset has at least two distinct pedagogical advantages:

Neutrality: Students cannot rely on prior biological knowledge, forcing them to focus strictly on character traits and data.
Ground Truth: As the creator, I have access to the “true” evolutionary history, including exact divergence times, fossil ages, and ancestral states.

My goal is to provide a modern framework for exploring parsimony, likelihood, and Bayesian inference, techniques that have mostly developed in the field of phylogenetics after the original Caminalcules were conceived. My “aliens” remain nameless for now, but I hope that after some feedback from the workshop we can come up together with something suitable

One of my alien creatures
Initially, I intended to generate the dataset exclusively through simulation. However, I realized that balancing a didactic, easy-to-analyze dataset with a fully automated pipeline would require several additional weeks of work. I ended up moving to a hybrid approach, simulating parts of my dataset and manually curating others. I did take the time to make something that was general enough so that I could possibly reuse it in a more ambitious setting or expanded into a proper scientific tool.
Coding (Phylosim)
The Github repository is here
The tool itself is a collection of scripts (temporarily named Phylosim) with 3 main modes:


T : To simulate species trees
The simulator produces phylogenetic trees using a birth death process (so, forward in time).  The idea that fossils “mostly” belong to extinct diversity that branches off the extant diversity is an important concept that for some reason is hard to grasp (even for reviewers of scientific publications, as I sadly had the opportunity to experience firsthand).


E: To simulate the evolution of traits
On top of the species tree, you simulate the evolution of traits. I wrote two probabilistic models: the first one was to simulate discrete characters using Markov Chains.  The user can define his own model, including as many states as he desires and different transition rates (in the same time units as the species tree). The second one was a model of Brownian evolution for continuous characters.


A: To manually add specific evolutionary events
This is an additional function that would allow me to pinpoint a specific branch and a specific point within the branch to add a trait. All species descendant from that point inherit that trait. Multiple traits can be added (creating nested evolution). This is the part where most of the manual curation happens.


Once the simulator was ready, I simulated a dataset of about 100 species, including extinct lineages. The resulting table was something as follow:









































Node in the Species TreeBodyMouthEyesColor RColor GColor Bn1010120140100n2111909590n312220120150
Some of the traits were simulated with the E mode: the eyes were simulated using a discrete Markov Chain. The colors were simulated using 3 independent variables that evolved following a Brownian motion. The other traits were controlled manually to create an example of evolution that was suitable for the classroom.
Art
It is much more fun to work with something visual. For that reason, I decided to create sprites for the different aliens. I had some help here! My sister did the drawings in Procreate using her iPad. We divided the aliens into multiple parts that could be easily combined:

The challenge here was making all parts compatible, meaning that any head could fit any antenna, any body would match any side appendix, etc. Once we have about 5 or 6 sprites for each body part, the rest was a matter of combining them. I wrote a simple Python script that would take every row of the table with the different traits and combine them into a single image. The original images were all of them grayscale: the color variables that had evolved were incorporated by applying a tint to the images. These were some of the creatures resulting from this procedure:

Creatures of an alien fauna
Preparing the material
I took all the images and rendered them using Gemini into a photorealistic image. The prompt I used was:

A photorealistic 3D render of the creature in the image, preserving all its features. The shot is a macro photograph on a solid white background with professional studio lighting. The skin is insect-like. Be as close as you can to the original image”

I thought of including also different textures as variables to evolve, such as slimy, hairy or spiky, but for the sake of simplicity did not go that way

I sampled 23 leaves from the simulated tree and added 7 fossils. I was strategic with the sampling, trying to cover most of the interesting diversity we had generated and avoiding species that were too similar to each other. Fossils were sampled from extinct lineages (at the end of the branch, an even better option would have been sampling somewhere before the extinction). Since the tree is measured in time units, I gave the different fossils an age.
For the sake of simplicity, I also changed the name of the species that were sampled (the simulator uses n1, n2, n3, etc to name the different nodes of the tree) to letters of the latin alphabet for extant organism and greek letters for fossil ones. Using a package I wrote to plot trees (Phylustrator) I also generated phylogenies for the full tree, the extant tree and the sampled tree. Everything is in the Github repository in the form of Jupyter notebooks.

The sampled tree, including the images of the common ancestors all over the tree. It includes also the timeline on the left
I spent quite a while putting all the images together in a document using Affinity (in hindsight, I should have also written a script for this). I made two PDFs, one with the original renders and another one with the photorealistic images.

The original renders
I printed the resulting images into photographic paper. I tried two sizes, A4 and A3. In A4 the figures are too small and important details are lost, such as the number of eyes. However, the figures in the A3 are a little too big. The idea is that the students put all the leaves of the tree along the border of a big white cardboard and they draw the phylogeny.
Discussing the evolution of traits
It really helps to use these figures in which the different parts are represented with different colors. Using Phylustrator it is easy to generate these plots that indicate with small squares the points of transition from one body to another body.

In the exercise, the students need to recognize that the aliens have multiple parts and that these parts are homologous. Some of them are very easy to notice: the body shape, the side appendices, the tails, etc. By comparing them it is relatively easy at least to identify the major groups in the exercise (WKLH, NUSM, etc). The challenging part is (I think!) to reconstruct the deeper relationships between the groups.
There is one trait that is misleading on purpose: the eyes. The eyes evolve in the tree using the next model:

Eyes evolution
The rate of change was set high enough to see multiple transitions across the tree. Due to the high rate of change, eyes (in isolation) are not a good trait to recover the phylogeny. There are a lot of cases of convergent evolution all over. The changes can be visualized in the next phylogeny:

Some pedagogical observations
I am planning to use the evolution of eyes to explain how probabilities are computed in a phylogeny, both forward for simulation and “backwards”, for likelihood inference. Many possibilities stem from here, from explaining the different parts of probability models to Felsenstein’s pruning algorithm. My goal is not a highly mathematical description of these ideas but a clear explanation that shows, first and foremost, to show the problems that scientists face when inferring phylogenies. I think very often lecturers spend way too much time focusing mostly on the techniques and algorithms that people have found to approach different challenges and not enough time to present the students the problems themselves. In my opinion, the correct thing to do is to invert the time devoted to each part: much more emphasis should be put on presenting the problems before they are given any solutions whatsoever.

Longer-articles/The-unfinished-houses-of.title: The unfinished houses of Peru
Longer-articles/The-unfinished-houses-of.content:
I wrote this article in 2024 in Peru when traveling there
I arrived in Peru. Leaving the center of Cusco, which boasts extraordinary colonial architecture, the rest of the city looks like a nuclear bomb hit it. Around 80% or 90% of the buildings are unfinished. Many are multi-story structures with exposed rebar sticking out of the top floor and unpainted facades missing their final layer of cement.
This is something many foreigners ask about upon arrival: Why aren’t the houses finished?
The answers Peruvians give vary, but the most frequent one is poverty. After speaking with many locals about this, I realized that for them, the situation is so natural that they don’t quite understand the foreigner’s surprise.
From my perspective (perhaps a euphemism for my own prejudices), the “it’s poverty” answer isn’t a satisfactory explanation. Let me explain. If a person has no money, they don’t build a three-story building and leave one unfinished. I can believe that some people might underestimate their budget when starting a project and have to leave it incomplete, but the sheer number of houses in this state proves that isn’t the explanation. Most people build this way on purpose.
To illustrate this better. A poor house looks like this.

That is not what I am referring to. I am referring to a typical Peruvian house that looks like this:

Therefore, poverty cannot be the only reason why people don’t finish building their homes.
Taxes for finishing the house?
One explanation that fits the data is that there is a tax on houses once they are completed. This would create a very strong incentive not to finish them. After following this lead for a long time, my conclusion is that while this tax is real (the so-called predial, which depends on the municipality), it is so small that it wouldn’t be enough to explain the observations. There has to be something else.
Complex Reasons
To understand the real reason, you have to dig deeper and, above all, let go of the preconceived ideas you bring from home. What is perfectly normal for us is not normal for Peruvians, and vice versa. This symmetric relationship is very important, and I will come back to this point later.
For clarity, I’ll summarize the main factors that explain this situation:


In Peru (as anywhere else), if you want to start a family, you look for a house. There are two ways to get one: buy it ready-made or build it from scratch.


Buying a ready-made house is tremendously expensive for most Peruvians.


Building from scratch is much cheaper than buying. This shouldn’t be surprising. Building materials and labor are not expensive.


To build a house from scratch, you first need to get some land. Doing this legally can be very complex, so most people simply look for a plot that isn’t built upon and resolve ownership through neighborhood agreements.


Once you have land, you can build in two ways: legally or illegally.


If you decide to build legally, you have to ask the municipality for permits (which are extremely expensive), hire an official architect, and so on. We will return to this point later. The result is that only about 10% of houses are built legally.


If you decide to build illegally, you hire a “maestro” (master builder) to do the work. You decide to invest all your savings (what else are you going to invest in?) and you also try to make it as big as possible because, in the future, you want extra space for relatives or to rent out. A house is an investment in the future.


If you ever want to regularize your house, you do it by bribing the official on duty, which is much cheaper than building legally. Having a perfectly finished house also signals that you have money to spare, which is not a good position for negotiating this bribe.


Building is so cheap that it costs more to put the final touches on your house (cement layer, paint, etc.) than to invade a new space and start the process again.


Is it cultural?
I think it is. Since almost everyone acts the same way, there is a certain inertia to copy others and absolutely no incentive to finish a house so it looks good. Doing so would make you stand out like someone painting a house fuchsia in one of the white villages of Cádiz.
Why don’t you get a loan to finish the house?
Several reasons, but the main one is that since almost everything is illegal, banks don’t grant loans because they have barely any guarantees of recovering them. Most Peruvians simply save what they can and invest it as soon as they can, distrusting anything that isn’t material and that they can’t physically control.
How do houses get water and electricity?
Currently, the government is responsible for this. Houses group together in neighborhood collectives and negotiate with the government to provide these services. It doesn’t matter that most are illegal because the government of the day has no capacity to refuse. There are so many illegal houses that they have no choice but to compromise or face a possible popular uprising.
The Surprise is Symmetric: The Case of Spain
One of the people I spoke to most about this (a builder) asked me questions about the situation in Spain. I found it hard to explain how things work there. Just as I couldn’t understand the unfinished houses, he couldn’t understand that people didn’t build them from scratch (which does happen, sure, but we all know it’s not the norm). Specifically, this person was surprised because:


People usually ask for a (huge) loan to access housing. 35-year mortgages have become normalized.


It is much harder to build illegally. You can run into serious problems if you do.


It is also very difficult to build legally.


Many people think it is crazy to allow new areas to be urbanized and leave it in the hands of individuals or private companies.


Many people do not want to understand, for ideological reasons, that houses get more expensive if you artificially limit construction.


People in Spain are starting to blame tourism. The economy in Cusco depends almost exclusively on tourism. Blaming your main source of income is like shooting yourself in the foot.


I don’t know which case is more absurd. The houses in Peru being built everywhere and unpainted, or the case of Spain (which we can extend to almost anywhere else in Europe), where people mortgage themselves for life to have something that, if the system allowed it, would be much cheaper and accessible to everyone.
I also don’t know which situation is more desirable. In Peru, the urban landscape is horrible, but people get houses to live in. In Spain, regulations keep the landscape pretty (and I don’t even think they succeed at that), with a human cost that is hard to exaggerate, where the biggest losers are the poorest. Let this not serve as a trap to fall into a false dichotomy. The choice is not between Peru or Spain; other worlds are possible. It would be enough to take steps in the right direction, being aware that the starting point is not the same in different countries.
The Mystery of Capitalism
Investigating this topic, someone recommended an excellent book written by a Peruvian economist, Hernando de Soto, which garnered praise from both sides of the political spectrum. Titled The Mystery of Capital, it deals with how capitalism works in the West but fails in many other places.
This book explains that for most of history, construction has been done privately. The states that succeeded in creating legislation that helps people (and not one that actively harms them, turning them into de facto criminals forced to pay the cost of acting outside the state) were those that took people’s properties and incorporated them into a suitable legal framework. A legal framework that allows them to use their property and do with it what they think best, whether renting it, selling it, opening businesses, or living in it. This is a complex process that requires a judicial system with guarantees, an agile bureaucracy, and taxes that do not distort people’s real preferences.
Hernando de Soto has spent decades studying the problem of poverty at street level. To understand the difficulties facing the poorest population, he decided to do an economic experiment. First, he asked different lawyers how long it would take to open a business, and everyone (based on existing legality) said it was a process of a few days. Second, with the help of a team of researchers, they opened a small business following legal channels (in Peru, with a single employee). To do this, a researcher had to:

Work 6 hours a day
For 289 days
The cost of registration was $1,231, which was 31 times the minimum wage in Peru.

Another experiment was to build a house legally:

It took 6 years and 11 months to obtain the land title.
Obtaining the legal title to the land took a total of 728 steps.
Obtaining the construction permit required 207 steps.
They had to visit 52 government offices.

In Spain, property rights are administered infinitely better than in Peru, which in practice ends up in the worst of all worlds. In Peru, you don’t have a state that provides certain guarantees, but one that forces you to solve your problems outside of legality, with the cost that entails.
The Housing Problems in Spain
In Spain, the problems are numerous but of a different kind. For example, limits on construction are so strict that there is barely any high-rise construction and hardly any new areas are urbanized. This artificially limits the quantity of houses built and drives up the price of housing.
Urbanizing an area is presented as something incredibly complicated that must be done by a series of “wise men,” as if for most of history cities hadn’t grown naturally, including many of the most beautiful cities in the world. Building skyscrapers, which would allow for increased population density in big cities, is presented as something almost impossible and crazy, taking decades, as if the Empire State Building hadn’t been built over 100 years ago in little more than a year.
There is also a general climate of insecurity, with a serious squatting problem (okupación) that helps neither the owners nor the most disadvantaged groups. The solutions seem to only be able to come from active government action, when in reality they are the main ones responsible for the lack of a buoyant market for construction, urbanization, and transport.
Allow industries to build more. Allow people to decide for themselves what they want to do with their property and let them do it with guarantees. Allow competition from transport companies, which will open up new areas to build. The request is simple and humble. It is the same one Diogenes made to Alexander the Great: Stand a little less between me and the sun.
The most tragic thing about this whole affair is that the measures frequently discussed to solve the housing problem (rent control, banning tourist apartments, creating new housing through subsidies) do not aim to solve the problem but to appease people who, for ideological reasons, prefer not to understand how the system works. Paraphrasing Hernando de Soto, the true enemy of progress is not the left or the right, but the status quo.
A Final Reflection
It is just as important to have a state that guarantees certain rules (compliance with free contracts between people, private property rights, security) as it is that the rules and regulations do not hinder the free action of individuals to carry out their life projects in the most appropriate way possible.
In both Peru and Spain, for different reasons, this is achievable, but it will depend on taking steps in the right direction. Currently, at least in Spain, we are going in exactly the opposite direction. Whether there is a change of course will depend mainly on a large number of people abandoning their prejudices and understanding that progress happens not by defending a tribe, but by facing problems objectively, making honest calculations of costs and benefits, and making the right decisions.

Random-thoughts/Are-species-natural-kind.title: Are species natural kinds?
Random-thoughts/Are-species-natural-kind.content:
I have always considered that species are natural kinds and organisms merely instances of a general class. However, I recently learned about the Ghiselin-Hull thesis and now I am not so certain. First I had to overcome some initial skepticism with their argument due to what I consider a poor choice of terminology (I am not a fan of using the term individuals as they do). After some reflection I think they are mostly correct and it is inaccurate to consider species as natural kinds. The mental experiment that convinced me is this: if we found a tiger on Mars, with the same stripes, claws, jaws and the same DNA as tigers on Earth, but had evolved independently by perfect convergent evolution, would we say that the tiger belongs to the same species that an Earth tiger? Most likely not. If tigers were instances of a class the answer would be yes.
Right now my epistemological position can be summarized in the following points.

Realism is correct. There are structures and processes in the real world (in the territory).
Those processes might create objects that share similarities.
Prototype theory is essentially correct; we classify objects into fuzzy categories based on similarities and differences.
Gold as a category refers to something in the real world. Species also refer to something in the real world. Both are valid categories.
Gold and species are different types of structures, the first one is the result as a static property of the universe, the second one is the result of many processes over time.
It makes sense to move the discussion beyond natural kinds vs artificial kinds and start talking about Dennett’s Real Patterns. Species might not be natural kinds in the traditional sense but they are Dennett Patterns (same for gold).

Following some recommendations by Gemini, I put a couple of books on my Amazon basket about this topic. One is The Species Problem: A Philosophical Analysis by Richard A. Richards. The second one is Natural Categories and Human Kinds by Muhammad Ali Khalidi. It would be interesting to see if reading them substantially changes my vision of the world.

Random-thoughts/Being-productive-vs-Feel.title: Being productive vs Feeling productive
Random-thoughts/Being-productive-vs-Feel.content:
Last week I spent a surprising amount of time working on the Yongle Dadian Collection, which is a collection of booklets that I am curating, on a wide range of topics I am interested in, from the evolution of spiderwebs to the development of greenhouses in Almeria. These are highly specific topics for which it is not easy to find a non-fiction book that could serve as a brief introduction.
The pipeline I am using is mostly automated, but still requires some manual curation and human supervision, it is not as easy as asking an LLM, “write about X”, so I found myself pouring an inordinate amount of hours into it. Then after a while I realized I was not putting enough time in other activities that I enjoy such as playing piano or reading books; I think that generating these booklets felt very productive but the real value lies in actually reading them, and doing something with them! So far I have completed 50, and I will stop there for now. If I manage to generate about 100 a year, and read them (the most important part!), I should be more than satisfied.

Random-thoughts/Moving-the-goalposts.title: Moving the goalposts
Random-thoughts/Moving-the-goalposts.content:
When someone is moving the goalposts this creates a very good opportunity to really understand what this person really believes in.
For example:
“I think that machines will be intelligent once they pass the Turing test”
A machine passes the Turing test
“Well, I think that machines are not that intelligent because they can’t count the numbers of r in strawberry”
Machines learn how to correctly count the number of r’s in strawberry.
“Well, I think machines can’t really think because they can’t find original proofs to mathematical problems”
A machine finds an original proof to a mathematical problem
“Well, I think machines can’t really think because…”
The story repeats
When someone keeps moving and moving the goalposts it is a clear signal that the original given reasons were not the real reasons why someone held an opinion.
What happens inside our skulls resembles more something like this, in two steps
-Step A: An opinion is formed based on a mix of inference (more or less explicitly) and emotions, and happens quickly and mostly subconsciously.
-Step B: We find the reasons that justify this first opinion. But these reasons are just posteriori constructions.
The person that keeps moving the goalposts does it because the first intuitions and emotions that “truly” explained their position (Step A) are still there and they have not gone away. The intuition could be something like “humans are really unique and what happens inside our skulls can’t be mechanical”. The problem in Step B: we are not that good at really introspecting inside our skulls and seeing why we believe what we do (and as Robert Trivers showed, there might be a strong evolutionary reason for this!).
I think we all can fall prey to this pattern, but some people seem to be more susceptible than others. If you notice yourself moving the goalposts, I think this is a good signal to really look into your own beliefs and try to formulate real goals/tests that would really change your mind if they were met.

Random-thoughts/New-year's-resolutions.title: New year's resolutions
Random-thoughts/New-year's-resolutions.content:
Since I turned 16, every single year on the 1st of January I sit down and I write a list of the things I would like to accomplish during the year. Normally, I like to include categories, with a long list of movies and books, places to visit, people I want to meet and things I want to be better at. Seeing my lists on the 31st of December is always very humbling. I fail at almost everything I tried to accomplish, because I vastly underestimate the amount of time that everything requires and the amount of energy and willpower that specific skills need.
Over the years, I have lost many of my lists… the ones written on paper end up (maybe accidentally) in the trash can and the digital ones lost in the memory of an old computer that for some reason I will never use again. But from time to time some of these lists reemerge and I can see what my past me set out to accomplish, and then, in general, I feel quite proud! It is true that most of the things I wanted to do over the years I did eventually, just not when I said I was going to. Over the years I managed to do many of the things I wanted to do when I was younger. I hope the trend continues into the future. In my current list there are a few things that for some reason I am finding some resistance to do: learning German, hitting the gym more often and learning a few piano songs. Maybe a way to put some more external pressure on myself is having this reminder here for my future self. We will see.

Random-thoughts/Painting-with-acrylic.title: Painting with acrylic
Random-thoughts/Painting-with-acrylic.content:
Today I have been painting a whale on a small wooden canvas. It is the first time I have really painted something in a long time and my first ever using acrylic. I found the experience relaxing and very pleasant, I will repeat it! The result is not totally bad, but I can do it better next time. The whale looks like this (the yellowish hue is due to the lighting).

Some of the things that went wrong were:

I printed the whale in black and white to transfer it to the canvas. Once I started transferring, I could not easily see the parts I had already transferred. Next time, print in light grey
The transfer paper was not very effective. I might not have attached it properly
I did the toning with an orange color that was not diluted enough.
I did not choose the colors wisely. The blue background was too similar to the color of the whale. I must be able to see these things happening in advance
I don’t think the background turned out especially nice because I didn’t plan it out beforehand
I was not systematic enough with the coloring. The colors had some clear and well defined layers, but I did not respect them. I think I need to be more intentional about the color layers
The black acrylic marker that I bought was way too thick and difficult to control for the size of the painting. Luckily enough, I had a thinner marker that worked perfectly
I am not sure I understood how to use the glazing

In general, I think it is good to have a list of steps because there were many things to do and it was easy to miss steps:

Prepare the drawing digitally
Make sure you have planned both the background and the subject. Think about the colors
Prepare the canvas by applying multiple layers of gesso and sand in between
Print the drawing in light grey
Make sure that both transfer paper and the drawing are well attached
Tone the canvas with a complementary color to the main color of the painting
Use a pencil to add anything missing from the image
Add matte medium
Paint the sides
Start painting, from back to front.
The back must look hazy and muted. Punchy colors for the foreground
Use layers. Use glazing to add shades
Paint from dark to light. Use shift and lift
Use the marker to write the lines.
Apply isolation coat
Apply varnish (2 layers, perpendicular)

Random-thoughts/Pushing-your-own-underst.title: Pushing your own understanding
Random-thoughts/Pushing-your-own-underst.content:
A couple of days ago I finished Timur Kuran’s “Private truths, public lies”. I found it  interesting but also very dense, with a very detailed explanation of a mathematical model that underpins most of the argumentation. I was under the illusion that I had understood most of it, or at least I had got the gist: people falsify their inner preferences to conform to a majority position, and this creates all sorts of distortions in the ideas that are discussed in society. Turns out there is much more to it. I gave the epub to Fable 5 (just before the ban, had to continue with Opus 4.8 after it), so that it would quiz me about the book and, oh boy, I was wrong. I had understood a very shallow version of the arguments but I had missed some of the most central insights and mechanisms at play. I explicitly asked the LLMs to be strict and poke holes in my understanding, and in a long Socratic conversation I managed to have a few “aha!” moments.
Reading a book alone gives you about 10% or 20% of gains. You get to spend some time thinking about the arguments, the anecdotes, the models: after that, you manage (with a bit of luck) to remember the main topic and a few of the examples.
A few years ago I discovered (yes, I know, who would have thought about it) that taking notes after reading the book or preparing some Anki cards gives you a much better understanding of the content and allows you to retain much more. Maybe the gains are about 50 or 60%.
This, discussing deeply the book with someone (something?) that “actively” tests whether you got a grip on the models there presented, yields gains that are probably of 80 to 90% of what you can extract from a book.
Of course, this slows down my reading rhythm a bit but I prefer quality over quantity, so I am certainly acquiring this new habit of having a deep discussion with the LLMs after reading something meaningful.

Random-thoughts/Recording-memories.title: Recording memories
Random-thoughts/Recording-memories.content:
For some reason I cannot quite explain, sometimes I feel the need to organize my thoughts about the past. On one occasion (in 2014) I recorded a summary of my life up to that point, not because I thought it was extraordinary and important to preserve, but because it gave me some sense of direction. That recording is most likely lost, and that’s fine.
These days I have felt the same urge, but I realized that if I wanted to record everything relevant or irrelevant that has happened in my life in the last 36 years, it would take me an extraordinary amount of time and energy to accomplish. I want to do it but I just don’t want it “that much”. Unless there is a way to reduce the cost, to at least an acceptable one that I am willing to incur. And surprise surprise, there happens to be one.
Nowadays, the audio transcription to text by AI is surprisingly accurate: it is not perfect, but it is good enough for what I want. I subscribed to a service called VoiceNotes that allows me to take voice notes. I installed an extension that allows me to send Audio messages to WhatsApp (the same way I would do to a friend), and the messages are automatically transcribed into text and stored online. Then, I used an Obsidian plugin that allows me to download all the markdown notes to my vault (and add some time stamp for them).
So now taking notes has become an incredible easy task. Talk about whatever you want, as long as you want (some of my notes are more than 30 minutes long), the machines will decipher the sound and translate it into text.

Random-thoughts/Risks-of-Cultural-Abunda.title: Risks of Cultural Abundance
Random-thoughts/Risks-of-Cultural-Abunda.content:
We live in a time with endless opportunities to consume all sorts of cultural products.
Movies, series, documentaries, books, comics, blogs, you name it. With the advent of AI, I expect the cultural production of our world will only increase. In such a world, there are at least two challenges that I think are worth considering at a personal level:


Choosing what to consume. It is too easy to consume whatever they are showing on Netflix, a random book with a catchy title that just became popular this year or a YouTube channel that puts some interesting content every day. Very often, we just slide into certain cultural spheres without realizing it. I would like to be agentic about this and decide consciously what I consume and what I do not. Even if I live until I am 100 years old, the amount of content I will be able to absorb is just a microscopic fraction of all the work created out there by all sorts of people across time and geography. For that reason, I think it is worth making that tiny fraction the best of the very best. I have always tried, but I think it is good to have a reminder to continue to strive.


The temptation to only consume. It is too easy to just want to consume culture. It is easy to be under the impression that everything worth saying, reading or watching has already been put forward by someone, somewhere. I do think this is mostly true. However, I could bet that most content creators who made anything at all started producing culture that they did not believe was worth paying attention to: they just did it in spite of certain embarrassment about the quality of their work. Also, I am a firm believer that the only way to improve at something is just doing the damn thing.
My teacher Jose Maria told me not long ago that I am an explorer, but only an explorer of the worlds that other people have created. This was undoubtedly a valid criticism and one worth listening to, so I decided to shut up, listen to his advice and do something about it. That something is this blog.

Random-thoughts/Using-the-wrong-baseline.title: Using the wrong baselines
Random-thoughts/Using-the-wrong-baseline.content:
When people say “there is a lot of …” or “there is not enough of …” they are implicitly comparing with some specific baseline. Being aware of that baseline is important because otherwise it can make you fall into some silly mistakes.
For example, when discussing the housing problem, many people think that “regulations” can’t really be the problem, because they look around and they see construction happening.
“Around my house there are many cranes!”
And the obvious question to ask is:
Compared to what? To the absolute absence of cranes? You do not know the amount of construction that would happen if regulations were not constraining the supply: the fact that house prices are so high today should already tell us that cranes are far from numerous. In most cases, they’re very few. So why compare with zero? Why not compare with the amount of construction that would happen if one place were on its way to becoming a city like Tokyo or Singapore?
Another example:
“The population is too high. This place can’t maintain so many people.”
Compared to what again? To empty space? To the population density of hunter-gatherer Australia? It might be. But many places on Earth have very high population density and remain very livable. Why would you systematically compare to very sparsely populated places?
Do not systematically use nothingness as the baseline

Random-thoughts/XY-and-the-Monkey's-Paw.title: XY and the Monkey's Paw
Random-thoughts/XY-and-the-Monkey's-Paw.content:
You have a goal, call it G.
To attain G, you think of a proxy P.
You ask an agent to give you the instructions for P.
The agent gives you long complicated instructions to solve P. You implement it, with a lot of time and effort.
You totally fail to see an alternative solution, because you were just focused on P.

For example:

You want to access your home, but you forgot the key. You call a friend who is very good at picking locks and he spends 30 minutes on the phone giving you complicated instructions on how to unlock that precise lock that your door has. After that, you spend 2h finding the right tools and picking the lock until you succeed. Then, you realize that you could have just called another friend who lives 5 minutes from you and has a copy of the key.

This pattern is called the XY problem. It is well known in technical support, where a user who wants to do X asks how to solve Y instead.
This is similar to the Monkey’s Paw problem. The Monkey’s Paw would be:

You have a goal G
To attain G, you think of a proxy P
You ask an agent to do P for you
The agent is wildly successful at implementing P. However P does not solve G, or it does it in a way that has unintended consequences.
You failed because you did not solve the real problem G, but a proxy

For example:

You want to go out with the prettiest girl in the class. You ask the Monkey’s Paw to give you big muscles so that you can impress her. The Monkey’s Paw gives you an abnormally massive deltoid that looks deformed. You impress the girl, but not in the sense that you expected. You fail to go out with the prettiest girl in the class

The pattern is similar, but not the same. In the XY problem, the problem is about efficiency. In the Monkey’s Paw problem, the issue is about unexpected consequences.
A minor difference in the way I presented both problems is that in the XY problem the user implements the solution and in the Monkey’s Paw, it is the agent. I think this is not really the fundamental distinction, and whoever implements the solution is actually irrelevant.
I have encountered the XY problem multiple times when interacting with AIs. Luckily, no Monkey’s Paw problems. For now.
A solution to the XY problem is making sure that your goals are clearly explicit at all times! Goals sometimes have a hierarchical structure, and some of them might still be there and not be necessary to clarify. Some of our goals are sometimes even not obvious to ourselves. For example, I’m working on some research now. I could present my goals to the AIs by saying:

My goal is to solve this very specific technical detail

However, this is easy prey for ending in a XY situation. A better one would be:

My goal is understanding better this general problem that exists in the field of microbiology
A subgoal is solving this very specific technical detail

A third option, which is still better could be:

My goal is publishing a paper in (at least) a mid-tier journal, in the next 6-12 months
The paper will deal with this specific problem
To solve this specific problem, I think we need to solve this technical detail. However, if there is a different alternative path for this, please let’s explore that

This last structure is much better because it gives enough context. Most of my previous failures have been about not giving enough context. Of course, one could give “too much context” and then end up reconsidering some fundamental decisions in life, but that’s out of the scope of this post.
